About us

Sustainable energy practitioners have long noticed energy access affects rural and urban populations’ livelihood, generation capacity, education attendance, health outcomes and overall quality of life. In response, SELCO India (for profit, social enterprise) created SELCO Foundation on 5th October, 2010 as a public charitable trust, with the mission to:
1. Systematically identify diverse needs of underserved communities, understand and define the role of
sustainability and energy in these communities.
2. Create and support innovative and sustainable solutions that positively impact well-being, education and livelihoods and work towards the alleviation of poverty.
3. Foster ecosystem development in the social sector through holistic thought processes in technology, finance, entrepreneurship and policy.

SELCO Foundation envisions a socially sustainable society: we seek to create avenues for asset building, enhancement in quality of life and wealth creation that will uplift deprived sections of society through sustainable development solutions. It uses soft funding and flexible capital to develop robust and field-proven technological and financial models in the field of energy and sustainability. It aims to generate public awareness about these models, while also building the ecosystem for the creation and delivery of such solutions. The foundation supports replication and utilization of these models in other deprived regions of India and the world, thereby achieving greater leverage on resources.

7,500 smallholder farmers. Livelihoods for 2,000 women. 2.5 lakh students eating nutritious food. A thriving ecosystem for climate-resilient millets. What do they all have in common?

Mahesh Londhe.

When his mother was diagnosed with diabetes, Mahesh started exploring healthier food choices. That personal experience led him to build Millets Now—an enterprise that combines entrepreneurial drive with a deep commitment to farmers, women and his wider community.

Decentralised renewable energy and efficient technologies have helped Mahesh take this work further: powering local processing, improving product quality, meeting growing demand and giving him greater control over his energy and growth.

If you’re working on millets, sustainable agriculture, clean energy, food processing, women’s livelihoods or farmer-led enterprises, we’d love to connect. Reach out to us to explore opportunities to collaborate.

1,900 Anganwadi centres across Karnataka are set to become more climate-resilient strengthening child care, nutrition and learning.

On September 9, 2026, SELCO Foundation and the Women & Child Development Department, Karnataka, have signed an MoU to jointly solarise these centres, supporting healthier, safer and more child-friendly Anganwadi centres and strengthening the environment for early childhood care, education, nutrition, child health and development.

As part of this effort, 1,500 lights will be installed across the centres, improving visibility and creating more conducive spaces for children. Alongside this, SELCO Foundation and WCD will work together to develop model Anganwadi centres, exploring how energy and infrastructure can better support maternal and child wellbeing and community services.

From reliable lighting to better spaces for learning and care, climate-smart solutions enhances everyday infrastructure that early childhood development depends on.

Video Series: Financing Climate-Smart Livelihoods

Clean energy can transform livelihoods — but making the right technology work for a household also depends on whether the financing works.

Chapter 2 — Decentralised Renewable Energy: What It Means for Financing — is now LIVE!!

A khoya producer in Belagavi had studied his market, found his buyers, worked out his margins.

Then he stopped. “We wanted to buy it, but finances were a major obstacle.”

Because DRE livelihood assets aren't something you pick off a shelf. They're panels, a battery, a machine, wiring and installation — all brought together at once, with an upfront cost that can exceed what a household earns in a month.

And the credit that reaches these families is often built around consumption. A wedding. A phone. Borrowing that draws on income.

What they need is credit that enables income — a livelihood that can become the backbone of a family.

That gap is what this chapter is about.

What if accessing an entrepreneurship opportunity didn’t mean navigating multiple systems alone?

For many Persons with Disabilities, livelihood and enterprise opportunities already exist. Yet access to finance, government schemes, assistive technology, skilling, machinery and markets can remain fragmented and difficult to navigate.

The PwD Entrepreneurship & Livelihood Mela, held on September 4, 2026, in Raichur, Karnataka, brought these pieces together in one place.

Designed as a convergence platform, the Mela brought together approximately 500 Persons with Disabilities, alongside government departments, financial institutions, technology providers, machinery vendors, training partners and existing PwD entrepreneurs.

From exploring viable livelihood models and assistive technologies to accessing guidance on schemes, finance and enterprise development, the Mela was designed to make the ecosystem easier to see, reach and navigate.

Importantly, the journey doesn’t end at the Mela. Aspiring entrepreneurs will be supported further through assessment, business planning, training, incubation, finance linkages and enterprise establishment under the PwD Entrepreneurship Development Programme.

Because inclusive entrepreneurship is not only about creating opportunities. It is about bringing the right support within reach.

Video Series: Financing Climate-Smart Livelihoods

Clean energy can transform livelihoods — but making the right technology work for a household also depends on whether the financing works.

Chapter 1 — Energy Costs in Low-Income Households: Why Financing Matters — is now LIVE!!

For a woman who spends her day working in other people's homes, reliable energy can mean running her own processing unit in the evening — and building a business of her own. For a person with a spinal cord injury, it can mean charging a delivery vehicle and earning independently.

But a machine only earns if the right one arrives, if there are buyers waiting, if someone lends for it, if someone repairs it when it stops — and if repayment falls due when the money actually comes in.

And unreliable energy already has a cost. A dairy farmer in Hubli was spending ₹5,000 a month on grid electricity and generator fuel. A small food unit in Puttur was spending ₹500 a day on diesel.

If families are already paying for energy, can finance help them invest in energy that helps them earn?

That question is where this series begins.

When disaster strikes, resilience means more than preparing for disruption. It means building health systems that can keep going through it.

Power cuts, damaged infrastructure and inaccessible roads can quickly turn a functioning health facility into one that cannot deliver the care its community depends on.

Climate-responsive healthcare creates autonomous, independent and resilient infrastructure that empowers communities. By keeping essential systems running when surrounding infrastructure fails, these solutions help health facilities deliver critical care to mothers, newborns and vulnerable populations, while remaining reliable lifelines for communities facing disasters.

A small enterprise. A determined entrepreneur. A sweeter way forward.

Six months into making jaggery, Soumya, an organic jaggery entrepreneur from Pandavapura, Karnataka, was already thinking about the future.

She saw an opportunity to turn her own sugarcane into something more, invested in her unit, and built a business around it. When unreliable power became a barrier, she found another way forward.

Today, her climate-smart jaggery unit produces 1,000–2,000 kg of jaggery and earns a profit of INR 46,109 (USD 481) a month, has built 3 new B2B relationships, and avoids 18 tonnes of CO₂e every year by moving away from diesel.

Sometimes, building a resilient livelihood starts with refusing to stop.

October 14, 2025

education, Global South, Grantee, Healthcare

(Pictured above: SELCO builds awareness among community members and individuals on impact, use, and maintenance of technologies, like solar panels.)

The SELCO Foundation is a nonprofit headquartered in India that develops and deploys clean energy solutions to improve livelihoods and increase access to healthcare and education in under-resourced communities.

SELCO follows an ecosystem approach, which aims at catalyzing both demand and supply by innovating on technology, financial, and ownership models. It does that from the bottom-up, building capacities among communities and relevant stakeholders, creating enabling conditions and influencing policy which allows for inclusive innovations to thrive.

SELCO uses soft funding and flexible capital to develop these models in the field of energy and sustainability, and its incubation program fosters local entrepreneurs in developing enterprises that deliver sustainable energy-driven solutions. This holistic approach looks at the enterprise ecosystem as a whole and develops crucial opportunities for social entrepreneurship.

For several years, SELCO has been a critical thought partner for The Lemelson Foundation in how to develop inclusive regional innovation ecosystems. The Foundation supported SELCO’s establishment of a model that applies a climate lens to poverty alleviation, and that promotes greater inclusivity in the transition to clean energy and within the Indian innovation ecosystem as a whole.

SELCO has spent a decade refining a replicable approach to strengthening enabling ecosystems for local ownership, development, adoption, and maintenance of sustainable energy innovations. They collaborate with local actors to address key ecosystem aspects like the supply chain of efficient technologies, affordable end-user financing, and local entrepreneur and enterprise development.

Uniquely, SELCO has access to three levels of stakeholders: Communities vulnerable to and impacted by climate change, ecosystem stakeholders serving and innovating on solutions for those impacts, and global stakeholders whose policies, commitments, and services impact the working model of ecosystem stakeholders.

SELCO has expanded their work from addressing energy poverty in India to supporting the creation of climate smart solutions that address poverty as a whole. Their work shows that climate action and economic justice can be part of an integrated economic development strategy, and can directly reach the communities that are most affected by climate change, but are often excluded from the benefits of the clean energy transition.

Overview

Introduction

While the development community initially doubted the notion of a viable business model for solar energy for the rural poor, the idea had gained many supporters by the 2000s. Solar energy, after all, seemed to offer a sustainable option to enhance rural development. Independent of unreliable grids or polluting generators, solar power could provide residential and commercial lighting, as well as power simple devices. And yet, numerous solar projects languished, others were abandoned, as the business model seemed to fail to deliver on its promise.

Though a long-time advocate of sustainable and Decentralized Renewable Energy (DRE) for the poor, Harish Hande was not surprised by how some large-scale efforts to deploy solar in development had gone awry. He founded SELCO India, a for-profit company, in 1995 and learned that introducing solar meant more than delivering a panel and a battery. Especially for the poor, solar had to come with an appropriate plan for financing and maintaining the apparatuses. Devices to be powered by solar had to be adapted to the output of the panels and there had to be demand for the services or merchandise produced. In short, an entire ecosystem had to be mobilized to support a DRE intervention.

Hande founded the SELCO Foundation (SF) to apply the insights gained at SELCO India to the problems of development writ large. In contrast to those who began with the objective of deploying as many solar panels as possible, SF stressed the importance of designing a system with the end user and their supporting ecosystem in mind. The Foundation worked with rural households, small technical organizations, financial institutions, and community organizations to test, pilot and scale particular interventions. For Hande, SF’s goal was not just to create various DRE solutions, but also to promote design thinking among development organizations and to provide what Hande described as “Lego Blocks” that others could put into place for their own development initiatives throughout the world. SF worked in many locales in India, but the Foundation targeted India’s rugged Northeast states as a test bed that could offer an instructive set of lessons.

While SF worked in many facets of development (e.g. health, education), the Foundation’s work on livelihood promotion presented an especially thorny set of challenges to their design approach – issues that needed to be solved in order to diffuse their methods to other organizations. SF’s experiences in the Northeast showed that the existing ecosystem to support microenterprises in a region could be disconnected, antiquated, and resistant to change. Therefore, rather than simply aligning civil society and technical organizations, the Foundation had to incubate support organizations so that they could in turn help microentrepreneurs.

The requisite complexity in the scope of projects would be an even more acute problem outside of India. Foundation staff recognized that taken-for-granted ecosystem pieces in India could be absent in other locations. The issue would be less of bridging gaps between existing entities but creating organizations and resources de novo. This represented a tall order for anyone trying to emulate SF’s approach - How would a designer of an intervention define a feasible scope for a given intervention?

Furthermore, to a greater extent than other verticals, livelihood promotion was culturally and geographically specific. SF faced the challenge of translating the experiences of the microenterprises it seeded in one region in India with a different set of livelihoods that were present in other parts of the country and of the world. What of SF’s experiences could be communicated with other development and DRE organizations?

Furthermore, other NGOs considered SF a special case as the Foundation had committed funders willing to look at the long-term progress of SF’s interventions holistically over time. More traditional funders and NGOs relied on narrower, short-term output metrics to measure progress. Should SF try systematizing the ecosystem approach and develop useful yardsticks to evaluate success, with an eye toward shifting how more traditional funders and NGOs approached development? If so, what might those metrics be?

Modal window for SELCO Foundation menu

Suggested Citation:

Jaan Elias, Morgan Yucel, Greg MacDonald, Tony Sheldon, "SELCO Foundation: Diffusing a User-centered Ecosystem Approach to Sustainable Livelihood Promotion," Yale Case 24-012, July 23, 2024.
